title: Discours exécrable des sorciers
author: Henri Boguet
modern_edition: Boguet, Henri, An Examen of Witches, trans. E.A. Ashwin, ed. Montague Summers, John Rodker, 1929
significance: Account by the senior judge of Burgundy who prosecuted approximately 600 persons; provides detailed evidence standards and legal procedures applied to witchcraft cases; important for understanding French prosecution practice.
summary: Boguet served as grand judge of the territory of Saint-Claude in the Franche-Comté and presided over extensive witch prosecutions from the 1590s onward. His Discours draws on his judicial experience to provide a systematic account of witch practices and prosecution procedure in seventy chapters. Part I addresses the reality of witchcraft and the devil's pact. Part II covers diabolical practices: sabbath, metamorphosis, harm to neighbors. Part III provides legal guidance including evidence standards, use of torture, and sentencing. The text is practical and detailed, reflecting hands-on judicial experience rather than scholastic synthesis.
clark_analysis: Clark uses Boguet alongside Remy and de Lancre as evidence for how judicial practice fed into and reinforced demonological theory: the cycle of prosecution experience and systematic writing created an increasingly elaborated and practically-grounded demonological consensus.
hutton_analysis: Hutton notes Boguet's evidence for the social dynamics of Franche-Comté prosecutions: the accused were predominantly poor women, the accusations often arose from community conflict, and the judicial machinery was locally driven rather than externally imposed.
ginzburg_analysis: Ginzburg examines Boguet's cases for evidence of folk beliefs that predate or diverge from the demonological template: the Franche-Comté material includes elements potentially connected to Alpine night-journey traditions that the inquisitorial framework reframed as diabolical.
key_arguments: Witches form real organized sects in league with the devil
Physical metamorphosis (wolves, cats) is possible through diabolical agency
Children can be recruited as witches by their parents and should be prosecuted
Judicial torture is justified and should be applied in stages
The judge's duty to God and society requires vigorous prosecution
influence_on_prosecutions: Boguet's text was widely cited in French legal contexts as a practical authority for prosecution procedure. His legal appendix (Instruction pour un juge) was separately reprinted and provided guidance that influenced prosecution practice in Burgundy and beyond.
scholarly_disagreement: The number of 600 prosecutions Boguet claimed has been analyzed by regional scholars; archival evidence supports high prosecution rates in his jurisdiction but the precise figure is debated. The Summers translation is considered unreliable. Monter's comparative study of the French-Swiss borderlands provides important context for Boguet's Franche-Comté prosecutions.
